# Commitment Spiral

A 36-week fictional capacity model. The opening scenario starts in week 6; reset returns to week 0. Run, step, or schedule policy changes. Fork pins the current course (including already scheduled policies); return to the fork allows the same intervention to be tried earlier or later. Every branch uses the same stateless seeded demand sequence. Dashed chart segments and the week-36 comparison are projections under scheduled policies.

Three levers control accepted demand, resistance to shortcuts, and protected recovery. Each week's effort balances across delivery, returned repairs, reporting, recovery and idle time. Fatigue reduces the next week's capacity. Overdue promises and lower trust increase reporting effort. Shortcut defects become visible two weeks after delivery; repair costs 1.7 effort points per defective point. Usable output subtracts both known and hidden outstanding defects.

The optional **Challenge the model** section changes repair cost (0.5–4 effort per defect), maximum capacity loss from fatigue (0–75%), and direct reporting effort per 10 overdue points (0–1.5). Defaults are 1.7, 45%, and 0.65. Applying assumptions pauses and replays **both** courses from week 1; it preserves the demand seed, policy histories, fork and selected week. Assumptions are shared across branches and persist through scenario/reset actions until explicitly restored. Ordinary and trust-related reporting remain even when the direct lateness cost is zero. Saved sessions and exports include the assumed values.

The model is deliberately small. Work is divisible and homogeneous; all new promises have the same two-week window. Coefficients, scenarios, trust and fatigue scales are illustrative, not calibrated. Demand does not respond to trust. No pricing, strategic value of commitments, hiring, cancellation or renegotiation. Outcome colours indicate the direction of a measure, not a universal best policy. Declined work is shown without assigning it a value.

`engine.js` is pure and independent of the UI. Run `node --test dist/commitment/engine.test.js` from the project root. Tests cover conservation, defect delay, seeded forks, intervention timing, opportunity cost, recovery, quality, changed feedbacks and comparable replay. Existing engine calls retain their defaults; `step` and `simulate` accept an optional fourth assumptions argument. Browser state is saved under `thinking-lab:commitment:v1`; export produces Markdown with policies, assumptions and actual/projected weekly data. No network or external dependencies.

Feature-detected WebMCP tools expose state, policy scheduling and simulation controls through `document.modelContext.registerTool`, with a `navigator.modelContext` fallback. Both synchronous and asynchronous registration failures are contained; runtime parameters are validated. Native browser support is not confirmed. The experiment works without that API. Chart data is also available as a native HTML table.
